issues.legal_issue: Whether a shrine associated with a charitable institution was a public temple under the statutory definition when the evidence did not establish that the Hindu community or a section of it used the shrine as of right for religious worship.
material_facts: The institution's grants were principally recorded as supporting its head or the distribution of food and alms to fakirs, sadhus, and travellers; the grants did not establish that the shrine was endowed for public worship.
The shrine was constructed after the original grants, and part of the institution's income was spent on worship and related expenses.
Witnesses for the appellants said they sought the head's permission to enter and described not seeing members of the public worship there; the Supreme Court accepted their evidence.
The Board's witness asserted that the shrine was public, but the Court considered his testimony unreliable, and no member of the Hindu public testified that worship there was a matter of right.
Visitors attended and participated in festivals, but the Court held that such attendance did not by itself establish a right of access.

The High Court had relied on the shrine's physical features and entries in the inam registers; the Supreme Court considered those entries in their full context and concluded that they did not establish a public temple.
issues.conclusion: The shrine was not a temple within the statutory definition because the Hindu community, or any section of it, was not shown to use it as of right for religious worship. The appeal was allowed, the Board's order was set aside, and the District Judge's order was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9(12) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926 required a place to be used for public religious worship and to be dedicated to, for the benefit of, or used as of right by the Hindu community or a section of it for religious worship. Public attendance alone does not prove use as of right, since visitors may be admitted to a private shrine. The presumption that temples are public in parts of the Madras Presidency is rebuttable and was weak for a shrine near the Presidency's boundary; see Mundancheri Koman v. Achuthan Nair. Inam register entries have substantial evidentiary value, especially where original grants are unavailable, but must be assessed in their full context rather than by accepting individual entries at face value; see Arunachellam Chetty v. Venkatachalapathi Guruswamigal. The statutory challenge proceeded under section 84(2).

rule.if: statutory_temple_classification_appeal and private_access_control_evidence and (no_evidence_of_public_rightful_worship or public_attendance_without_proof_of_right)

predicates.statutory_temple_classification_appeal: An appeal challenged a determination that a shrine or religious institution fell within a statutory definition of a public temple.
predicates.private_access_control_evidence: People who entered the shrine sought the institution head's permission, and witnesses reported no observed public worship there.
predicates.no_evidence_of_public_rightful_worship: No member of the relevant religious community testified that the community or a section of it had a right to worship at the shrine.
predicates.public_attendance_without_proof_of_right: Visitors attended the shrine or its festivals, but the evidence did not establish that they attended or worshipped there as of right.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns whether a shrine is a statutory public temple, evidence of private control together with no proof of public worship as of right, or attendance without proof of such a right, means the shrine is not a public temple.
